implementation_notes:
# Shared iterative divider for `cores/bench`

`DIV`, `DIVU`, `REM`, and `REMU` share one EX divider. It captures the forwarded operands on issue and processes a 35-bit padded dividend in seven cycles of five restoring steps. EX transfers the sign-corrected result through the existing EX/MEM register, adding eight cycles to each divide or remainder instruction.

EX waits for an older data access to advance before launching. While the divider runs, the fetch PC and ID/EX register hold and EX/MEM receives bubbles with their side-effect controls cleared. EX retains the issued operands for RVFI after the forwarding sources drain. Completion is consumed on the EX/MEM transfer edge. The `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` arithmetic substitutes use the same schedule.

The restoring steps naturally produce an all-ones quotient and the original dividend magnitude for a zero divisor. Issue logic suppresses quotient negation for that case and still sign-corrects the remainder. Signed `INT_MIN / -1` produces `0x80000000` and a zero remainder through the normal datapath. Divider tests live in `test_div_unit.py` so the existing cocotb runner can exercise the clocked divider and combinational ALU as separate tops. A guarded include in `core.sv` makes the pipeline types available for the requested glob-order lint command.

## Local verification

- Verilator strict lint passed with hardware arithmetic and with ALTOPS.
- Cocotb passed 72 tests across six suites. The divider suite covers the original arithmetic vectors, additional operand ranges, consecutive launches, backpressure, and reset. The pipeline test holds a store for three cycles and checks one accepted write, one retirement per instruction, forwarded operand reporting, and immediate use of the quotient.
- `formal/run_all.sh` passed all 53 single-channel checks, including liveness and all four divider instructions. The gate used ALTOPS and ready buses. Cocotb and co-simulation exercised the hardware arithmetic and memory stalls.
- Co-simulation passed for selftest and the three random programs with ready buses and with both stall generators enabled. CoreMark validated all five reference CRCs, retired EBREAK, and reported no out-of-bounds access.

## Gowin and CoreMark

| Measurement | Baseline retest | Iterative divider |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Median Gowin Fmax | 5.442 MHz | 48.196 MHz |
| CoreMark cycles between markers | 4,491,485 | 4,491,485 |
| CoreMark iterations per second | 12.12 | 107.31 |

Gowin placement options 0, 1, and 2 reached 47.541, 48.196, and 48.196 MHz. Option 0 used 2,664 logic cells and 565 registers. Its worst reported path crossed the register-file and ALU datapath at 26.329 ns. The divider feedback path reached 26.309 ns in the same placement.
lesson: - 2026-11-21 hyp-20261121-001-r1s0 (improvement, +785.40%): Rare operations on the shared EX forwarding path can limit the clock for every instruction, so moving DIV/REM into a shared iterative divider raised median Gowin Fmax from 5.442 to 48.196 MHz with unchanged CoreMark timed cycles because no DIV/REM retired between the timing markers.

title: Move DIV and REM to a shared iterative execute unit
motivation:
Bench's baseline closed at 5.442 MHz median Fmax and 12.12 CoreMark
iterations per second. The reported 199.837 ns, 156-cell path runs from a
writeback destination through forwarding and the EX ALU toward the data
address path. The four combinational division and remainder expressions
feed the same result mux as ordinary ALU operations and are the likely
source of the deep logic. Every instruction pays their timing cost.
An unmodified baseline cosim with both bus stalls enabled reproduced
the logged 4,491,485 bracketed cycles and passed CoreMark CRC validation.
Its 2,922,015 timed retirements included zero DIV, DIVU, REM or REMU
instructions.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU into one blocking, clocked execute unit. At
launch, capture forwarded operands and the operation, and register the
operand magnitudes and sign flags. On the first update clock, compute
the top radix-4 digit from the dividend magnitude's top two bits and
register the divisor multiples D, 2D and 3D. Among nonzero divisors,
only magnitudes one, two and three can yield a nonzero first digit. On
each of the next five clocks, cascade three radix-4 digit steps to
consume the remaining 30 bits. A step appends two dividend bits to the
partial remainder and uses three parallel trial subtractions to select
the largest multiple that fits. Use 34-bit divisor multiples and 35-bit
subtracts to preserve the full trial value and detect borrow. Select
the quotient or remainder, apply its sign and handle divisor zero and
signed overflow before the existing EX/MEM transfer. Keep the result
stable until that transfer.
This adds seven cycles with ready buses, leaving margin in the existing
ten-cycle liveness window for a redirect or load-use bubble. Use the same
issue and completion schedule for ALTOPS, with the four existing
opcode-specific arithmetic substitutes.

Hold fetch and ID/EX for the divide, allow older MEM/WB work to drain, and
inject bubbles into EX/MEM until result transfer. Give an older blocked
data request priority over divider launch and EX/MEM writes. Snapshot
the forwarded source values for RVFI so draining the pipeline cannot
change the reported operands. On transfer, send the result through the
existing result forwarding and single-channel retirement path exactly
once. Reset cancels any pending divide. Ordinary instructions retain
their existing execute latency, and loads and stores retain their bus
handshake and alignment rules.

The registered recurrence should remove the full-width combinational
divider from the ordinary execute path and reduce LUT pressure. The
measured instruction mix implies zero direct divider stalls inside the
timing window. Divider stalls during initialization can shift the bus
backpressure sequence entering that window. At the baseline cycle
count, 5.70 MHz would clear the acceptance threshold and 8.17 MHz would
reach the forecast. Measure the actual bracketed cycle count and median
Gowin Fmax after implementation.

title: Predict hot control transfers with a single-read tagged target buffer
motivation:
The bench core fetches fall-through until EX resolves a control transfer. Each
aligned taken branch or jump normally discards one fetch opportunity because
IF feeds ID/EX without a separate IF/ID register. CoreMark repeatedly visits
loop branches, calls, and returns. The baseline's 5.442 MHz median Fmax is
limited by the forwarded ALU path, so the predictor must earn its gain in
marker-bracketed cycles while keeping the fetch feedback path short.

Add a 64-entry direct-mapped branch target buffer indexed by fetch PC[7:2],
with a full PC[31:8] tag, a word-aligned target, and a two-bit saturating
direction counter. A valid tag hit with the counter's high bit set selects
the stored target in parallel with the existing PC+4 calculation. Learn
taken conditional branches and JAL/JALR from EX, using the most recent
resolved target. Initialize a newly allocated conditional entry to weakly
taken and strengthen or weaken matching entries on outcomes. Install legal
aligned jumps as strongly taken. Train once per advancing valid EX control
instruction and suppress training for traps. Reset the valid bits and leave
the payload arrays unreset to allow distributed RAM inference.

Use only the fetch-indexed table read. On an accepted fetch, register that
instruction's lookup hit and counter alongside the IF PC update for use by
EX training one stage later. If EX writes the same index on that edge,
capture the new counter and determine the captured hit by comparing the
writing PC tag with the fetch PC tag. Use this bypass only for training
metadata. The next-PC prediction uses the pre-edge lookup. Hold the captured
metadata during dmem backpressure so it stays paired with ID/EX.

Keep EX authoritative and compare its resolved next PC with the current
fetch PC, which is the successor selected when that instruction entered
ID/EX. Check every advancing valid instruction so stale entries also recover
on non-control instructions and traps. Correct predictions need no flush.
On a mismatch, bubble ID/EX and redirect to the resolved PC even if imem is
stalled. During an older dmem stall, hold the PC and ID/EX and defer both
recovery and training until EX can advance. Advance on a predicted path
only when the current fetch is accepted. Keep the full resolved PC for RVFI
and preserve the existing link value, misalignment traps, and memory gating.

A scratch RTL prototype with both bus stalls enabled reduced the canonical

option 0 used 12,571 LUT4s versus 12,312 at baseline. The implementation
needs about 5.31 MHz median Fmax at this cycle count to beat the champion

enabled. A directed cosim also held a loop-exit branch and a changing-target

verified the wrong-path store sentinels.

implementation_notes:
# Bench branch target buffer

## Implementation

- IF uses a 64-entry direct-mapped BTB indexed by PC[7:2] with a full PC[31:8] tag, a word-aligned target, and a two-bit saturating counter. Reset clears entry validity. Tag, target, and counter arrays use the same fetch index and infer RAM in Gowin.
- EX trains advancing legal control transfers. A taken branch allocates a weakly taken counter on a miss, strengthens it on a hit, and records the resolved target. A matching not-taken branch weakens the counter while preserving the last taken target. JAL and JALR install strongly taken entries. A same-index write forwards the tag match and new counter to the registered training metadata. The current prediction comes from the pre-edge lookup.
- Hazard logic uses a single fetch-accept signal for the IF PC update, predictor metadata capture, and ID/EX admission. An older dmem stall holds all three and defers training and recovery. EX compares its full resolved next PC with the current fetch address for every advancing valid instruction. A mismatch bubbles ID/EX and redirects even with imem unready. RVFI and recovery use the same EX PC resolution.
- The IF PC register stores the upper 30 bits and supplies the two aligned low bits at the interface. ID/EX establishes validity on admission directly. The EX/MEM bundle carries the resolved PC used for retirement.

## Verification

- Verilator lint and all five cocotb runners passed. The directed pipeline tests cover bubble-free taken prediction, loop-exit and changing-JALR recovery across both bus stalls, wrong-path side effects, and the same-index training bypass followed by a stale non-control prediction.
- Local single-issue formal passed all 53 checks on the first attempt.
- Cosim matched selftest and all three random programs with and without both bus stalls. CoreMark passed the canonical CRC checks with both stalls enabled.

## Timing and fitness

- CoreMark measured 4,186,330 marker-bracketed cycles for 10 iterations, a 6.79% reduction from 4,491,485.
- Gowin placement options 0, 1, and 2 measured 5.240, 5.533, and 5.533 MHz. Option 0 used 12,183 logic cells. The median yields 13.22 iterations/second, about 9.0% above 12.12.
- The worst setup path crosses operand forwarding and the ALU before reaching dmem. Placement option 0 measured below 5.31 MHz, so the placement median matters for fitness.
lesson: - 2026-11-21 hyp-20261121-003-r1s2 (regression, +9.08%): Benchmark fetch predictors on the current champion RTL because the single-read tagged BTB saved 6.79% of CoreMark timed cycles by avoiding taken-transfer bubbles, a gain outweighed by the older combinational DIV/REM ALU limiting median Fmax to 5.533 MHz against the iterative-divider champion’s 48.196 MHz.

title: Shorten execute timing paths at the current pipeline depth
motivation:

implementation_notes:
# Bench execute timing

The multiplier uses one unsigned 32-by-32 product from the forwarded register operands. `MUL` still transfers its low word in one EX cycle. The three high-word instructions capture the unsigned high word and signed correction sum on launch, register their difference on the next edge, and hold the result until EX/MEM accepts it. High multiplies add two EX wait cycles. They share the divider's EX wait policy and the registers that retain the launch operands for RVFI. ALTOPS uses the same schedules and preserves all eight substitution formulas.

The divider seeds four quotient bits and the remainder at launch, then runs seven groups of four restoring steps. It computes the signed dividend magnitude prefix independently of the 28-bit tail and uses the raw divisor to detect magnitudes below 16. The first timing run showed a critical path through a serial four-step seed. The final seed processes two bits at a time. The upper two bits use a small case split, and the lower two bits try one, two, and three copies of the divisor in parallel. Divide and remainder still add eight EX wait cycles, including for zero divisors and signed overflow.

Fetch passes the raw instruction and readiness to decode. Redirect and load-use squashes clear ID/EX validity on capture. Load-use detection requires both a valid EX load and ready fetch data. Redirect retains priority over PC holds. Invalid EX entries cannot redirect, launch arithmetic, or pass memory or register-write controls downstream. The top-level memory ports and single-channel RVFI contract are preserved.

## Local checks

- Verilator `-Wall` lint passed for both hardware and ALTOPS. All seven cocotb runners passed, including the original multiply vectors, held high-word completion, the divider seed boundary, and unready and squashed fetches.
- `formal/run_all.sh` passed all 53 single-retire ALTOPS checks on the final RTL, with zero failures or fix retries. Hardware arithmetic was exercised in cocotb and co-simulation.
- `make cosim TARGET=bench` passed selftest and all three random programs with zero-wait and stalled buses. Stalled CoreMark completed in 4,491,485 timed cycles with all five canonical CRCs and `Correct operation validated.`

implementation_notes:
# Elastic fetch with early redirects

Fetch now has a two-entry fall-through FIFO that stores each instruction with its full PC. It admits ready fetch words using registered capacity, lets ID consume buffered words during instruction bus stalls, and refills on a one-entry pop. A full queue defers new admissions until the cycle after a pop. After buffering the final mapped instruction word, fetch holds its address until that word issues or a redirect clears the queue.

An issuing JAL or taken BEQ/BNE can redirect fetch from ID when its target is aligned. BEQ/BNE use the write-first register-file values when neither source has a pending nonzero writer in EX or MEM. The early target adder uses a B- or J-format offset. The issued instruction carries a bit into EX to suppress a second fetch redirect. EX computes the architectural next PC, link value, and misalignment trap, and handles the remaining transfers. A second bit in EX records a redirect sent while data backpressure holds that entry. EX redirects take priority over ID issue, and load-use bubbles leave the queued instruction available for the next cycle.

## Local verification

- Strict Verilator lint passed in both hardware-arithmetic and ALTOPS modes.
- The standard single-channel formal gate passed all 53 checks on the first run. It used the standard ALTOPS configuration and ready buses.
- All 78 cocotb cases passed across six suites. Directed pipeline tests covered queue fill and ordered drain under both bus stalls, load-use interlocks, early JAL link forwarding, BEQ/BNE decisions and operand fallback, wrong-path discard, alignment traps, and the instruction-window boundary. A JALR held behind a blocked store redirected once, with one accepted store and exact RVFI PCs and order.
- Co-simulation matched selftest and three random programs with ready buses and with both stall generators enabled. Stalled CoreMark retired EBREAK with no out-of-bounds access and printed `Correct operation validated.` All five CRCs matched (`0xe9f5`, `0xe714`, `0x1fd7`, `0x8e3a`, `0xfcaf`).

CoreMark took 4,195,317 cycles between the MMIO markers for 10 iterations. Gowin placement options 0, 1, and 2 measured 46.059, 48.391, and 48.391 MHz. Option 0 used 3,120 logic cells and 659 registers. The 48.391 MHz median gives 115.35 iterations per second, 7.49% above the 107.31 iterations per second champion. Index it with PC[7:2] XOR PC[13:8] at fetch and training to spread branches

so the counters can map to distributed RAM. Start unused entries at weakly
taken for backward branches and weakly sequential for forward branches.

direction. Predict every aligned JAL to its direct target on the first
visit. Resolve JALR in EX through the existing forwarded operand path. The
instruction determines whether a prediction applies and supplies its target,
so table aliasing changes only the direction of a conditional branch.

Predecode the B/J opcodes in IF, including the six legal branch funct3 values,
and form the PC-relative target for the current instruction alongside PC+4.
Use word-address arithmetic with the low target bits carried separately for
alignment. Add the low 19 word-address bits to the sign-extended 19-bit
word offset. Precompute the unchanged, incremented and decremented values
of PC[31:21] in parallel. Select them by applying the low carry minus the
offset sign to the high part. Use this full computed target in EX for

# Bench EX datapath implementation

implementation_notes:
# Predicted-path fetch queue

IF runs the folded-index 64-entry predictor at the instruction bus and holds up to four ready instructions in a shift queue. Each slot carries the full PC, instruction, six-bit index and selected direction. Decode bypasses an empty queue. A load-use bubble or EX hold retains the decode head, and a full queue can refill on the same edge that decode consumes its head. An advancing EX correction clears all occupancy and squashes decode even when the bus is unready.

The fetch and issue lookups use separately inferred RAMs. The fetch RAM mirrors each counter's high bit and reads the pre-edge direction. The queue head selects the issue index independently of its prediction bit. An advancing, nontrapping conditional branch trains both copies, and its write forwards into a same-index issue snapshot.

IF qualifies the 19-bit word sum for source window, target window and halfword alignment. A fall-through from the last mapped word enters ID/EX directly, then parks fetch until EX advances with the resolved successor. EX reconstructs the full RV32 direct target in word units and uses the immediate's bit 1 for alignment. The resolved successor drives RVFI and recovery, and JAL and JALR links remain PC+4.

## Timing changes

- Queue shift and refill candidates are calculated alongside EX correction. Correction has priority over the occupancy update and decode admission. Keeping the correction out of the payload enables removed a path through EX comparison into the queue flops.
- EX shares the forwarded base-plus-immediate sum between JALR and the registered load/store address. MEM uses the address register for the bus and byte-lane alignment. This removes the general ALU result selector from the data-memory setup path. The bus address during cycles without a memory strobe can differ from the champion.
- The divider and the EX-to-IF recovery path now limit or nearly limit Gowin timing. The four queue slots contribute to the increase in area. Placement option 0 used 3,323 reported logic cells, 1,037 registers, 16 LUT RAMs, six block RAMs and two DSPs.

## Local verification

- Strict Verilator lint passed with and without the cocotb VPI switches.
- `bash formal/run_all.sh` passed all 53 single-channel ALTOPS checks on the final logic, including liveness. The first attempt's `pc_fwd_ch0` trace expected retirement at `0x000ff8e4` after a load-use bubble and observed PC zero. Yosys treated the packed-struct array as bit slices. On the first retry, Yosys rejected the typedef argument to `$bits` in the packed-vector array declaration. Switching to `$bits(fetched)` passed the second retry. The final timing changes passed the suite again.
- All seven cocotb runners passed, including 23 pipeline cases. The directed cases cover loop recovery over an unready bus, full refill, buffered issue during unready fetch, same-index training, last-word parking and full-width out-of-window resolution.
- `make cosim TARGET=bench NRET=1` matched the ISS for selftest and three random programs with zero-wait and stalled buses. Stalled CoreMark passed all five canonical CRCs, reported `Correct operation validated.` and performed no out-of-bounds memory access.

implementation_notes:
# Resolved-backedge loop replay

IF tracks one inclusive loop of up to 128 words. EX signals an advancing, aligned, taken conditional backedge and IF captures its PC and target independently. A contained backedge keeps the current descriptor. Ready bus words stage for refill into a synchronous block RAM containing the instruction, page bit, and 18-bit prediction target with its eligibility bit. Replay checks the full page address, the indexed word's page bit and validity, and any read/write collision.

The three-entry distributed RAM queue carries the word PC, instruction, and taken prediction. Bus and replay share the folded direction table and supply separate target candidates. EX computes the full architectural direct target and supplies resolved RVFI next PCs. A replay that advances while imem is unready holds the outstanding request address through its ready response. IF discards that response and resumes requests at the producer PC. Registered EX recovery overrides the held address, squashes younger work, and disables replay in the corrected cycle.

An accepted store overlapping the descriptor clears word validity. FENCE.I clears the descriptor and any pending refill, then restarts fetch at its sequential successor. The directed tests cover replay across two 512-byte pages, draining and overriding held requests, ordered retirement on loop exit, and a store patching a warmed loop while a younger FENCE.I waits behind the store.

## Timing changes

The first placements exposed long paths through the replay collision check and EX forwarding. The final RTL records the RAM write index and compares it with the registered producer index in the following cycle. It also computes last-word parking eligibility without waiting on the bus target sum. Decode registers the raw source-to-destination matches and EX qualifies them with the post-trap write enables. MEM registers the selected architectural write value before forwarding. These timing changes preserve the instruction and arithmetic issue schedules.

# Implementation notes

Fetch now adds the 18 word-address bits below the 1 MiB boundary. The low carry minus the offset sign selects the original, incremented, or decremented page for the full 32-bit B/J target. `PC+4` uses the same split and shares the incremented page. The halfword alignment check still qualifies prediction. [Fetch RTL](cores/bench/rtl/if_stage.sv)

The window check factors the three original-page comparisons into an upper-eleven-bit match and a separate low-bit match. This gives the same page-zero result for pages `0`, `1`, and `0xfff`, including 32-bit wraparound. The factored implementation gave the best measured median in the local Gowin trials. The fetch direction lookup and pending-update comparison use the XOR hash of the selected PC. Each PC candidate is hashed before applying the existing address masks.

The directed test checks long JALs in both directions, an aligned backward branch from the last mapped word, and an untaken branch with a trained taken counter whose target is `0x00100000`. It checks the request sequence through a stalled recovery, as well as retirement order, successor PCs, and link values. The test passed on both the original and revised RTL and failed with the prediction range gate disabled in a scratch copy. [Pipeline test](cores/bench/test/test_pipeline.py)

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the native recurrence with a fixed-schedule Goldschmidt divider
built from a synchronous reciprocal seed ROM, registered multiply stages,
and an exact residual check. Keep the existing EX launch, eight update
edges, completion hold and consume protocol, and early EX/MEM retirement.
Keep the ALTOPS arithmetic and its matching schedule.

At preparation, capture operand magnitudes, zero detection, and the
quotient and remainder signs. On update 1, left-normalize the nonzero
divisor into Q0.32 and register the shift s. On update 2, read a synchronous
1,024-entry ROM addressed by the ten bits below the leading one. If i is
the upper eleven bits of the normalized divisor, the 13-bit Q1.12 seed is
floor(2^23 / (i + 1)). On update 3, multiply the dividend and normalized
divisor by that seed. Store the 35-bit numerator n0 from bits [44:10]
of the dividend product. Store the 25-bit denominator deficit e0 by
complementing bits [34:10] of the divisor product and adding one when
bits [9:0] are zero. This takes the low 25 bits of 1 minus the scaled
denominator, rounded down. Both registers have 34 fractional bits.

On update 4, truncate e0 to 22 fractional bits to form f. Update the
numerator to n1 = n0 + floor_Q34(n0 * f). Compute e1 = e0 - f +
floor_Q34(e0 * f) in parallel. This keeps the upward rounding of the
refined denominator while using a narrow product, and e1 fits in 15 bits.
On update 5, form n2 = n1 + floor_Q34(n1 * e1). On update 6, register the
provisional quotient q by shifting n2 right by 34 - s from its integer
representation. Also register A - D and A >= D for the original operand
magnitudes A and D. On update 7, register q * D and the signed quotient
candidates for q and q + 1. The seed and both correction factors keep
the scaled denominator at most one, and numerator truncations round down.
The initial deficit is below 0.00122, and e1 is below 2^-19. Accounting
for denominator and numerator rounding at Q34 puts the real quotient
estimate in the interval [A/D - 0.90, A/D], so its floor is either the
correct quotient or one less.

Select q + 1 exactly when A >= D and q * D <= A - D. Use A - q * D or
(A - D) - q * D for the remainder and apply the dividend sign. The product
fits in 32 bits because the guess never exceeds the exact quotient.
Override a zero divisor with the all-ones quotient or original dividend
remainder. Preserve INT_MIN / -1 via the 32-bit quotient result. All
result registers and signs must stay stable until consume, with reset
canceling any active instruction. The existing divider handshakes retain

implementation_notes:
# Goldschmidt divider

The bench divider captures forwarded operands at launch, captures magnitudes and signs at preparation, then completes on update seven. Its datapath uses a synchronous 1,024-entry reciprocal ROM, two fixed-point refinements, and a residual comparison that chooses between the provisional quotient and its successor. The remainder candidates apply the dividend sign by ordering the subtraction operands. Divide by zero returns an all-ones quotient or the original dividend. Signed overflow preserves the low 32-bit quotient.

The denominator deficit takes bits `[34:10]` of the negated product. This is equivalent to complementing the upper slice and adding one when the lower ten bits are zero. The second numerator refinement stores only bits `[34:3]` because denormalization always discards at least three bits. Bounding the seed error at the lower endpoint of each ROM interval and accounting for the Q34 truncations bounds the real quotient underestimate below 0.884 for every nonzero divisor. The exact comparison therefore needs at most one increment.

The first placements exposed timing paths in fetch and low MUL. Fetch now tests the high address candidates for zero in parallel with the target calculation. EX selects low MUL at the final result mux and retains its one-cycle EX schedule. The divider handshake retains completion hold and reset cancellation, the ALTOPS schedule, forwarded RVFI operands, and early single-channel retirement.

| --- | ---: |
| 0 | 79.652 MHz |
| 1 | 83.861 MHz |
| 2 | 83.861 MHz |
| Median | **83.861 MHz** |

Placement 0 used 4,317 logic cells, 1,625 registers, 40 LUT RAMs, 5 block RAMs, and 9 DSPs. Its longest reported setup path runs from fetch recovery selection to the fetch parking register.

Gowin emitted `EX3780` on the ROM initialization loop index. The placed design inferred one `pROM`. I checked the initialization bits against the reciprocal formula for all 1,024 entries in each of the three generated bitstreams.

# Bench load-to-equality-branch bypass

- A legal BEQ or BNE can issue immediately after an aligned load to a nonzero register when either source matches the load destination. Every other pair keeps the existing load-use interlock. Data backpressure still holds the load and its dependent branch through acceptance.

implementation_notes:
# Pipeline branch resolution past issue

Ordinary conditional branches compare forwarded operands in EX. EX/MEM holds the comparison and one-hot recovery enables alongside the sequential and direct candidates. Each candidate carries its fetch-window, last-word, and direction-index metadata. IF selects the registered correction while the core discards speculative ID/EX work and admits the corrected response. JAL, JALR, and non-branch boundary recovery still trigger from EX.

A legal BEQ or BNE can issue immediately behind a matching load with a nonzero destination. The branch saves its ordinary forwarded operands and both source-match bits. In MEM it compares against the formatted load value in MEM/WB if the load wrote its destination. A trapped load leaves the saved operands in effect. Both matching sources compare equal. The MEM result controls the branch's next PC, trap, and RVFI operands.

A registered late correction suppresses both younger slots, including their memory requests, backpressure, bypasses, arithmetic launch, and branch training. MEM preserves the retiring branch for one cycle to use the freed WB slot. It also retains the load bypass value across a surviving branch so a deferred divide can still use its original source selection.

Ordinary predictor updates can reach the pending counter at the EX edge when no older update is waiting. This preserves predictor visibility for a corrected fetch that aliases the branch index. Otherwise the update follows the branch into EX/MEM. IF prioritizes older updates and queues the younger update when two surviving branches resolve together.

The timing iterations moved ordinary recovery qualification onto the EX/MEM edge and selected the direction index in parallel with the fetch address. ID starts the direct-target sum using two parallel word slices, and EX combines them before registering the candidates. MEM registers the selected late target and correction together. The ALU uses 16-bit carry-select ADD and SUB and one-hot EX result selection. The multiplier and divider keep their existing latencies.

- Local formal on the selected RTL has 51 passing checks. `pc_fwd_ch0` and `reg_ch0` are still solving, with no counterexamples reported. An earlier snapshot passed all 53 checks. # Registered Bench fetch head

The five-entry IF queue now decodes from a fixed head register. Four circular tail slots use one-hot read and write pointers. A queued issue promotes the oldest tail entry, and an accepted producer fills the head when it would otherwise be empty. Tail payload capture can run ahead of append. Occupancy and the write pointer publish the captured word only when the append commits. Full occupancy denies incoming fetches for the entire pop cycle.

The load-use interlock compares the EX load destination with both raw source fields of the head and both raw bus fields in parallel. Effective head occupancy and bypass validity qualify the comparisons. Registered recovery clears the logical queue and restarts its tail pointers. The corrected response can bypass immediately or populate the fresh head during an issue hold. Replay, stale responses, boundary parking, and FENCE.I retain their original admission rules.

The implementation also separates producer PC selection from the acceptance enable. ID zeros unused fallback operands before EX, EX compares branch operands in two halves, and low-word MUL captures the DSP result separately from the ordinary EX/MEM result. These changes improved the queue-only median of 89.629 MHz while preserving instruction and arithmetic latencies. Directed tests check a pop from full, concurrent promotion and append, a buffered load-use hold, and ready and stalled corrections with wrong-path stores in the queue.

implementation_notes:
# Predicted direct-target prefetch

Fetch reads two 16-entry instruction banks when it accepts a taken B/J prediction. Each bank has one word-PC parity. Two parallel narrow sums select the target and following word, including an odd-to-even index wrap. Each returned instruction has a mapped word-PC tag and is registered with its index and validity. Matching bus data has first priority, followed by the existing PC+8 replay slots and then the target pair. The pair advances fetch by one word and uses the existing replay enqueue and stale-response handling.

The fill window follows the first two producer positions after the taken prediction. Only accepted sequential bus words enter the staged write path. Each bank rejects a lookup that coincides with a write to the same index. Reset and FENCE.I clear bank and pair validity and cancel pending fills. The target banks stay idle during the PC+8 RAM sweep. The last mapped word still parks on bus acceptance.

The registered EX recovery request predicts sequentially. If it stalls, fetch adopts the corrected address as its registered producer. The ordinary predictor then uses that producer for both target sums and direction lookup. EX continues to resolve taken transfers and alignment traps.

The directed pipeline test covers both target parities, the index wrap, a held pair behind a full queue, a ready bus match, stale acknowledgments during second-word replay, same-index tag misses, and a simultaneous bank read and write. The existing tests also cover the corrected first fetch followed by trained predictions and FENCE.I with warmed code.

The timing changes keep the PC page register off the replay enable, compute the last-word target test alongside the full target sum, and compare EX branch operands in parallel byte groups. Ordinary EX recovery clears the held pair and the fill window. The tagged bank entries remain available for a later taken bus prediction.

title: Learn two-step successors for fetch replay
motivation:
The bench champion scores 252.90 CoreMark iterations per second at
89.983 MHz over 3,558,019 timed cycles. Its replay RAM returns a word
two cycles after lookup, so reading PC+8 works on sequential runs
and leaves a gap on taken transfers. Round 12's direct-target banks
saved 1.92% of timed cycles. Learning the address two accepted fetch
words ahead can point the existing replay read across a taken branch
before the branch word itself reaches the producer.

producer PCs. For accepted words A, B and C, record C under the low

sequential observation clears that index. Read the hint from the
registered producer's word PC in parallel with the bus predictor.
A valid hint supplies the word address for the existing synchronous
replay RAM. An invalid entry selects PC+8. Store the hint valid bit

sweep. Keep hints disabled until that sweep finishes. The hint index
may alias. The replay RAM's address tag and the slot's full producer
PC match still qualify every replayed word. Carry its instruction,
taken bit and precomputed successor from the same tagged record.

ordinary issue holds, and break that history at registered EX recovery
so an old wrong path cannot train a link to the corrected path. Keep

state. Train and replay within the mapped instruction window and leave

priority, the held bus address and stale-response discard, immediate
EX squash and the registered corrected bus request.

successor and its boundary flag at fill time. Keep the replay-slot
match separate from the bus predictor. Compute B/J predictions from

title: Issue tagged replay hits through the empty-queue fetch bypass
motivation:
The bench champion always writes replay hits into its fetch queue and
issues them on a later edge, even when the queue is empty and decode
can take a word immediately. A scratch profile counted 86,526 replay
accepts with an empty queue and no issue hold during CoreMark. Giving
these hits the ready bus word's fall-through behavior saved 24,467
marker-bracketed cycles in a scratch build.

hypothesis.motivation:
The bench champion always writes replay hits into its fetch queue and
issues them on a later edge, even when the queue is empty and decode
can take a word immediately. A scratch profile counted 86,526 replay
accepts with an empty queue and no issue hold during CoreMark. Giving
these hits the ready bus word's fall-through behavior saved 24,467
marker-bracketed cycles in a scratch build.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Stage one replay payload for possible direct issue. While the current
producer runs, nominate its sequential PC+4 and read that replay bank
using the incremented low two word-PC bits. Register the nominee's full
word PC, valid bit and instruction/prediction payload. If the existing
RAM lookup publishes into that bank on this edge, stage the incoming
payload when its PC matches the nominee and invalidate the nominee on
a conflicting replacement. Clear the staged valid bit on reset and
FENCE.I. This makes the stage a copy of the slot as of the producer
update edge. In the following cycle use the existing replay eligibility
and a full producer-PC match to authorize the staged word. Keep the tag
qualification off the wide instruction mux. ID can start operand reads
from the registered payload without waiting for the current PC to select
among four slots. Compute load-follower checks on the staged instruction
in parallel with the checks for the bus and buffered head.

Give the corrected or ready bus word and any older queued entry their
existing priority. If the queue is empty and ID can take the staged
replay word, advance the producer once and skip the queue write. A
replay hit that misses the staged nominee follows the existing enqueue
path. If ID is held or needs a load-use bubble, enqueue the accepted
replay word once with its PC and prediction metadata. Preserve the
held bus address and stale-response discard even when the accepted
replay bypasses the queue. Keep the full-tag check, RAM read/write
collision guard, reset and FENCE.I invalidation, boundary parking
and correction flush.

The unrestricted combinational bypass passed canonical stalled CoreMark
in 3,360,708 cycles and all eight ready/stalled RVFI traces. Its Gowin
placements measured 87.820, 89.342 and 89.342 MHz, limited by the replay
bank selection into ID operand capture. Registering only the bank
selector slowed fetch feedback in scratch. Staging the payload uses the
sequential nominee and keeps the resolved next-PC path off its input.
The staged version's coverage and Fmax are unmeasured. Target a median
of 94 MHz, which clears the 4.6% margin even at 3,385,175 cycles. Run all
three scored placements and the unmodified correctness gates.

implementation_notes:
# Staged replay through the empty fetch queue

- IF reads the replay bank for the producer's sequential PC+4 and registers the full word PC, validity, instruction, and predicted-taken bit. A same-edge lookup publish supplies the staged payload and a conflicting tag clears validity. Reset and FENCE.I clear the stage.
- A staged hit uses the normal replay admission conditions and a full producer-PC comparison. The tag checks qualify issue separately from the instruction mux and parallel load-follower classification. The live replay slot still supplies the target and the fallback queue payload.
- Corrected responses, older entries, and ready normal bus responses keep their priority. A direct replay advances the producer without writing a queue slot. An interlock, an issue hold, or a staged miss takes the original enqueue path. Stale request tracking follows replay acceptance in both cases.
- EX registers the combined conditional-branch correction bit alongside the existing predicate and target controls. This shortens recovery selection into the added IF instruction mux and preserves the existing recovery edge.

The directed pipeline tests check direct issue, physical queue-write suppression, load-use and dmem-hold fallback, ready bus priority, matching and conflicting refills, stale-response discard, an unstaged fallback, and FENCE.I invalidation. They check RVFI PC order and exact operands and results.

The initial staged RTL passed all 53 checks. Directed simulation covers the post-sweep replay cases because the formal wrapper holds imem ready throughout its 20-cycle bounded checks.

successor in parallel can cover taken and sequential fetches with

motivation:
The champion's tagged PC+8 replay slots cover sequential fetch well,
but the stalled CoreMark profile counted 199,584 timed cycles with
an empty queue and no usable instruction response outside recovery
and issue holds. Misses cluster around recurring producer PCs.

lookahead leaves a gap, including landings after taken transfers.

# Stall-trained fall-through replay

The fetch stage adds three synchronous copies of a 256-entry direct-mapped table. They share a staged write and read the PC+4, B/J target, and B/J target+4 indices in parallel. Each returned word crosses a second register with its full in-window word key. The publication register rejects reads that collided with a write.

A fetch gap marks the current producer until it advances or recovery replaces it. An accepted bus response with a fall-through prediction fills a marked entry. A ready matching bus response has first priority, followed by PC+8 replay, then stall replay. Stall replay advances the producer and uses the existing queue and held-response discard logic. It selects the precomputed sequential successor when the normal producer would otherwise hold. Reset and advancing FENCE.I cancel staged fills and start a 256-cycle sweep.

The timing variant separates fetch-page updates from the low-word successor mux and computes each upper bit of a short-offset load address from the raw word and its carry. Both changes preserve the original result and cycle timing.

The directed tests exercise first and second landing words, ready-bus priority, alias rejection, same-row collisions, stale responses, JALR recovery, and FENCE.I cancellation and invalidation.
